aerolog.title: AERO-LOG — Autonomous Drone for Emergency Medical Logistics
aerolog.intro: Proof of concept for an autonomous quadcopter dedicated to emergency medical logistics, built by a team of six at Efrei. A fully custom three-layer architecture: an ESP32 mini flight controller for real time, a Raspberry Pi 5 with a Hailo-8L accelerator for perception, and a ground station for supervision. I led the embedded firmware and the drone's flight bring-up.

objective.title: Objective
objective.text: Prove that a low-cost autonomous quadcopter can carry a 500 g medical payload and land on a visually detected target, under human supervision

timeline.title: Duration
timeline.text: Efrei Innovation Project — April to July 2026

team.title: Team
team.text: Six students across three majors — project lead and embedded systems owner

context.title: Where it started
context.p1: In France, 23,294 patients were on the transplant waiting list in January 2026, and only 6,154 transplants could be performed in 2025 — around seventeen a day. On the journey of a graft, a sample or an urgent drug, every minute saved counts, yet that transport depends entirely on the road network: congested in cities, sometimes cut off in disaster areas.
context.p2: The need is anything but theoretical. In a European trial run in Belgium to move a graft between two hospitals, the drone took 10 minutes against 21 by car — roughly twice as fast, simply by rising above the traffic. In France, a kidney travelled the 60 km between Nantes University Hospital and La Roche-sur-Yon hospital by drone in July 2026, in 36 minutes. AERO-LOG explores the same idea at student-demonstrator scale, on a low-cost platform with no off-the-shelf autopilot.
context.p3: The scope of the proof of concept is stated explicitly: the payload is simulated by a 300 to 500 g inert mass, flights take place on authorised ground under supervision, and no real biological product is carried — such a use would require medical, technical and regulatory clearance well beyond the project.
context.stat1: patients on the transplant waiting list in France, January 2026
context.stat2: transplants performed in 2025, around 17 a day
context.stat3: faster than a car on a graft transfer between two hospitals

role.title: My role on the project
role.badge: Project lead and embedded systems owner
role.p1: I coordinated the team and owned everything low-level: designing the flight board, integrating the sensors, calibration, and actually getting the drone airborne.
role.p2: On the firmware side, that covers high-frequency IMU reading with a complementary filter, the cascaded PID stabilisation loop (attitude then angular rate), quad-X mixing to the four ESCs over DSHOT300, ELRS/CRSF radio reception that always takes priority, and a watchdog that falls back to manual control if the onboard computer stops responding.
role.p3: I also specified and implemented the interface between the onboard computer and the flight controller, working directly with the vision and navigation team building the embedded perception on the Raspberry Pi.

item1.text: Flight board, sensor integration, calibration and test campaigns

technical.frame: Custom-redesigned quadcopter frame, four brushless motors and their ESCs
technical.fcu: Custom ESP32-based board acting as a mini flight controller

perception.title: Embedded perception
perception.caption: A single perception pass onboard the Raspberry Pi 5: depth map, occupancy grid, person detection, ArUco marker reading with its pixel offset, operator gesture — and the resulting navigation command.

step1.title: Pre-flight
step1.text: Checklist from the ground station: battery, sensors, GNSS fix and radio link. Any anomaly is reported to the operator and blocks arming.

step2.title: Take-off
step2.text: Controlled climb under supervision, with stabilisation handled end to end by the ESP32 mini flight controller.

step3.title: Cruise
step3.text: GNSS waypoint navigation, ground height measured by ultrasound and compensated for attitude, obstacle avoidance through optical flow.

step4.title: Final approach
step4.text: Guidance switches from satellite to vision as soon as the ground marker is detected and its relative pose estimated.

step5.title: Precision descent
step5.text: The descent is closed-loop on the distance and angle measured relative to the marker, targeting a landing error below 2 m.

step6.title: Release and return
step6.text: The release servo is commanded by the ESP32, then the drone returns to its starting point. Every state transition is logged so runs can be replayed offline.

realtime.title: Linux is not real-time
realtime.problem: Stabilising a quadcopter requires a deterministic loop around one kilohertz. On a Raspberry Pi, the Linux scheduler introduces unpredictable latency — more than enough to lose the aircraft.
realtime.solution: Split into three layers, with real time strictly delegated to the ESP32, which does nothing else — IMU, PID, motor mixing, watchdog — and always keeps radio priority. The Raspberry Pi is limited to attitude and thrust setpoints, vision and navigation.

link.title: Making the computer ↔ flight controller link reliable
link.problem: A text format such as JSON was too expensive to parse on the ESP32 for a fixed-rate stream, and MAVLink meant carrying a full stack for a very narrow need.
link.solution: An in-house protocol, aerolink: compact binary frames protected by a CRC16-CCITT over UART, watchdogs on both sides and automatic fallback to the radio if the computer goes silent. A Python decoder ships alongside the firmware for debugging — with the rule, learned the hard way, of always deploying firmware and decoder together.

mixing.title: Mixing sent to the wrong motors
mixing.problem: The firmware inferred each motor's position from its wiring order. Roll and pitch corrections were therefore sent to the wrong arms: a defect invisible on the ground, but fatal at take-off.
mixing.solution: A bench test campaign with propellers removed, identifying motors one by one from a web interface embedded in the ESP32. Because the mixing was written with symbolic position names rather than indices, the fix came down to a single line.

results.title: Where the prototype stands
results.p1: On the hardware side, the electronic board and the frame were custom-designed and assembled end to end at Efrei's iLab, after two test iterations — and the drone flies. On the software side, the autopilot is in place: give it waypoints and an altitude and it holds them under supervision; real-time telemetry and the operator dashboard work, as do manual takeover and failsafe. Perception runs on the target board: person detection, ArUco code reading and a depth map, all from the RGB stream alone.
results.p2: The limit is acknowledged: perception and control remain two separate blocks, not yet closed into a loop. Precision landing under 2 m and end-to-end payload transport depend directly on that. Total prototype budget: €541, of which €404 was funded by a grant and €137 came from hardware the team already owned.

done.title: Achieved
done.text: Take-off and stable flight, real-time telemetry, control dashboard, visual target detection.

ongoing.title: In progress
ongoing.text: Autonomous waypoint navigation: the autopilot holds heading and altitude, still to be consolidated in flight.

todo.title: To do
todo.text: Precision landing under 2 m, and flight with the 300 to 500 g payload onboard.

next.title: Next
next.text: Dedicated range sensors and 3D mapping, for navigation the drone chooses rather than follows.

skills.title: What the project taught me
skills.p1: AERO-LOG had me practise real-time embedded work under real conditions: high-frequency sensor reading, a stabilisation loop, filtering propeller noise out of the derivative term, and above all the discipline of testing in stages — arming, motors, PID, link — all carried out with propellers removed before any flight.
skills.p2: It taught me to design the interface between two worlds that do not run at the same pace: a deterministic microcontroller and an application-level Linux. That means a protocol designed for corruption, joint versioning on both sides, and fallback behaviour defined before it is needed.
skills.p3: Finally, coordinating six students from three majors — Embedded Systems, Data & AI, Business Intelligence — was the most formative part of the project: making firmware, perception and value analysis converge on a single product, against shared deadlines.

about.title: About
about.intro: Engineering student passionate about embedded systems, IoT, and electronics. Discover my journey, skills, and experiences.
about.bio1: I'm Matéo Repulles, a Master's student in Embedded Systems & IoT at EFREI, after completing my preparatory classes and Bachelor's degree at CESI. Passionate about electronics and firmware development for several years, I've had the opportunity to work on various projects ranging from drone validation to the design of electronic systems integrating additive manufacturing.
about.bio2: My approach combines solid theoretical training with concrete practical experience. Whether developing firmware on STM32, designing a PCB on KiCad, or debugging a real-time system, I enjoy tackling technical challenges and learning new technologies.
about.bio3: Beyond my studies and professional experiences, I'm also involved in the maker community, a member of the MakerCesi board, and a participant in WorldSkills for additive manufacturing. My hobbies include guitar, photography, 3D printing, and FPV drones.
